title: Supplemental Comments of Georgia Power Company et al. on the timely and cost-effective integration of large-load customers to support growth and enable economic development under RM26-4.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                  )
Interconnection of Large Loads to the             )                 Docket No. RM26-4-000
Interstate Transmission System                    )

                             SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF
                              THE SOUTHERN COMPANIES

       Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission” or “FERC”)

October 27, 2025 Notice Inviting Comments in the captioned proceeding, Georgia Power

Company (“Georgia Power”), Alabama Power Company (“Alabama Power”), and Mississippi

Power Company (“Mississippi Power”) (together, “Southern Companies”) submit the enclosed

Supplemental Comments for the Commission’s consideration. Southern Companies re-

emphasize their support for timely and cost-effective integration of large-load customers to

support growth and enable economic development and bolster the nation’s national security, in a

way that protects existing customers, as called for in the Secretary of Energy’s Advanced Notice

of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”).

       As detailed below, Southern Companies are connecting large load retail customers

quickly and efficiently, while protecting customers from cost-shifting, as identified in the

ANOPR and the President’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge. Southern Companies’ progress

towards “speed to power,” while protecting other customers, is a direct result of our state-

regulated, vertically-integrated planning and rate structures. Southern Companies respectfully

request that the Commission allow Southern Companies to continue building on this record of

success and progress towards the ANOPR’s goals, while preserving the historic jurisdiction of
 our state regulators over retail customer connections, the terms and conditions of which are

inextricably embedded in our bundled rate mechanisms.

I.      SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

        Southern Companies commend the Commission for its continued focus on large load

issues and the importance of timely, affordable, and reliable infrastructure development needed

to support growth and economic development. The ANOPR has sparked a critical national

discussion about how best to achieve these objectives. Consistent with the President’s Ratepayer

Protection Pledge, Southern Companies have been executing with speed to get power to large

load customers, with a goal of ensuring that families and small businesses benefit from that

growth and continue to receive reliable and affordable electric service. Southern Companies

submit the enclosed Supplemental Comments to augment the record of this proceeding and

provide the Commission updated information on successful large load integration initiatives in

Southern Companies’ service territories.1

        A.      Updated Success Data

        In their Initial Comments in this proceeding, Southern Companies reported Georgia

Power’s initial successes in integrating large loads, including that Georgia Power had already

successfully obtained Georgia Public Service Commission (“Georgia PSC”) approval of three

large load contracts, representing 1,900 MW of new load.2 Since this proceeding opened,

Southern Companies’ success has continued at a remarkable pace.

         As of April 2026, 32 large load customers have committed to receive approximately

15,600 MW of electric service from Georgia Power, including executed Contracts for Electric

Service for 9,572 MW of large load. In the near term, Southern Companies are finalizing 6 GW

of additional large load connection agreements across Alabama and Georgia.3 Also, 10 of these

32 large load projects are already online, with another 11 currently under construction.

        Southern Companies supplement the record in this proceeding with this data to provide

the Commission with the most current information, so that it can tailor any action in this

proceeding in a manner that propels, and does not hamper, such success in the Southeast and

elsewhere.

        B.      Elements of Southern Companies’ Success to Date

        In their Initial and Reply Comments, Southern Companies explained how they have

successfully integrated large loads in their service territories with a focus on speed and

affordability for all customers.4 Southern Companies explained that their vertically-integrated

structure and integrated resource planning process enable them to plan for and serve large load

customers by holistically combining generation, fuel, transmission, and distribution planning.5

This coordinated framework operates through state-regulated bundled retail service obligations

and integrated planning processes that align generation expansion, transmission development,

fuel planning, and retail service commitments within a unified regulatory structure. In addition,

Southern Companies explained that this structure rests on a foundation of effective state

        In Georgia, for example, with the approval of the Georgia PSC, Georgia Power Company

has implemented several mechanisms aimed to protect existing customers, including minimum

termination protection, and regulatory review and accountability for customer-specific

        C.       The Benefits of State-Driven Integrated Planning

The importance of Southern Companies’ integrated planning process to their large load programs

cannot be overstated. Serving large loads requires a holistic analysis of system conditions and

solutions to arrive at a prudent generation expansion and capital investment plan that balances

 speed, reliability, and affordability. Unlike regions that rely principally on fragmented market

structures or separated transmission and resource planning functions, Southern Companies’

planning framework permits coordinated evaluation of generation, transmission, distribution,

fuel supply, customer commitments, and retail service obligations within a single integrated

planning process subject to state oversight. Southern Companies’ integrated planning processes

take into account projected load growth, potential generation expansion, transmission build outs,

distribution investments, retail service obligations, fuel planning, and large load contracting that

are evaluated through coordinated processes under state regulatory oversight. Southern

Companies’ experience demonstrates that coordinated state-regulated planning structures can

support more timely generation development and reduce interconnection delays relative to

regions currently experiencing substantial queue backlogs and infrastructure constraints. These

differing regional conditions support preserving flexibility for frameworks already providing

coordinated and timely infrastructure development. For example, after Georgia Power

completed its triennial integrated resource planning process in 2022, and in response to growing

demand from large loads, including data centers, Georgia Power filed an off-cycle Integrated

Resource Plan Update in October 2023 as allowed by GPSC rules, requesting 3,300 MW of new

generation capacity. By April 2024, the Georgia Public Service Commission approved Georgia

Power’s total requested capacity and guaranteed downward pressure on customers’ rates for

years 2026-2028, further demonstrating the effectiveness and flexibility of state regulation to

adjust to changing circumstances, and an emphasis on speed for large loads and affordability for

all customers.




                                                  5
30184901.2
         Further, Southern Companies’ integrated resource planning process, vertically integrated

structure, and existing regulatory regime, have yielded no generation interconnection queue

backlog. These results highlight the significant differences between regions and the need for the

Commission to act in a way that preserves efficient state-led frameworks and allows companies

like the Southern Companies to keep executing on our—the Southern Companies, FERC, and the

Administration—shared objectives of quickly bringing power to all customers as reliably and

affordably as possible.

        D.       Affordability as a Centerpiece

        Affordability has been a central tenet to Southern Companies’ successful integration of

large loads to date. Southern Companies have integrated large volumes of new loads in a

manner that not only protects existing customers from additional costs, but actually benefits

these existing customers through allocating fixed-cost recovery across a broader customer base.

The successful components detailed above – namely, minimum terms and bills, protective

termination provisions, and appropriate collateral protection – have provided a reliable

framework under which new large loads will not be subsidized by other customers.

        In December 2025, the Georgia PSC voted to approve an agreement with the Public

Interest Advocacy Staff and Georgia Power that certified the construction of 9,885 MW of new

energy generation, almost all of which is expected to come online by 2030, much of which to

support new large load customers. This is one of the largest single generation expansions by a

company in U.S. history. The Georgia PSC concluded that its order protects existing ratepayers

from increased rates, even if the data center projections do not come to fruition.8 In fact, these

 new generation resources will ensure durable integration of large loads and are projected to result

in at least $1.6 billion in savings for Georgia customers (equivalent to anticipated savings for the

typical Georgia ratepayer of $100 per year) when Georgia Power files its next base rate case.

        As further evidence of this successful approach to affordability, Georgia Power

committed to a three-year base rate freeze. This rate freeze was made possible in large part by

Georgia Power’s success in signing up large load customers in conjunction with the rules and

regulations implemented by the Georgia PSC that ensure large load customers pay all of the

costs incurred to serve them.9 Alabama Power also recently announced it will enact a rate

stabilization program through 2027, which is expected to yield customer benefits as Alabama

Power integrates large load projects.10 Southern Companies’ proactive actions are aimed at

creating downward pressure on rates, which not only helps protect existing customers from

subsidizing large loads, but helps them to share in the benefits of that tremendous growth.

II.     CONCLUSION

        Southern Companies again commend the Commission for its attention to this historic

challenge. We respectfully suggest that any federal initiative that comes from this proceeding

preserve well-functioning state-led frameworks that can help deliver speed and affordability.

The record of this proceeding demonstrates significant regional differences that may justify more

reforms in some areas that have not yet seen the type of success that has occurred in the

Southeast. Indeed, various regions face differing operational structures, regulatory frameworks,

resource mixes, and interconnection challenges, and targeted reforms may be appropriate in

certain markets. Southern Companies are similarly aware of the difficult jurisdictional issues

 presented in this proceeding, as previously raised in their Comments.11 Given the success of

state-regulated integrated resource planning and bundled retail service frameworks in integrating

large load customers, such as in Southern Companies’ territories, a one-size-fits-all rule would

be counterproductive. Federal reforms should not inadvertently impair state-regulated planning

and retail-service frameworks that are already rapidly developing generation, transmission, and

customer-specific infrastructure needed to support large-load growth. Any federal reforms

adopted in this proceeding should preserve the flexibility for states and vertically integrated

utilities to continue to use coordinated bundled-service structures that are already delivering

timely infrastructure development, customer protections, and reliable service. To the extent the

Commission determines that additional near-term federal reforms are appropriate, those reforms

should focus principally on regions where wholesale market structures, transmission service

constructs, and Commission-jurisdictional processes are directly implicated.
